source.title: Reference-Grafting Matches Fine-Tuning at Eliciting Sandbagged Capabilities
source.authors: Linh Le; Hong-Fu Tan; David Williams-King

page_placements.theme: Hidden capabilities (password locks, sandbagging, circuit breakers) recovered by SFT or activation edits

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests elicitation of intentionally sandbagged model organisms, not recovery after unlearning. Its activation-edit results are an analogy about hidden capabilities, not tests of the unlearning methods or attacks in the claim.
record.gate_note: No unlearning method is applied, and the study does not test recovery after unlearning by fine-tuning, activation ablation, quantization, or prompting alone. It reports related results on sandbagging, which are recorded as findings about a different construct under fits_no_version. The cited WMDP work and other related-work results are not this study's results.
record.test_reason: No unlearning method is applied or evaluated. The study elicits capability from deliberately sandbagged model organisms (password-locks, prompt-induced, GRPO-trained, circuit-broken) by activation reference-grafting. Its WMDP results measure recovery of a trained suppression lock, not recovery after unlearning, so none of versions A–F is tested. The suppression is induced on purpose and is a different construct (sandbagging) from unlearned knowledge.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that in their organisms sandbagging is held in a few superposed circuits. Grafting those circuits' coordinate to the honest reference reverts it, matching fine-tuning elicitation at forward-pass cost. Circuit-breaking defeats this and every fixed map they test, though it gates rather than erases the capability. They also stress that the withholding axis is mechanism-specific: it transfers across datasets but not across induction mechanisms.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses password-, prompt-, or RL-induced sandbagging organisms and activation reference-grafting; it does not apply an unlearning recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes depend on the sandbagging mechanism and whether its suppression is a static, linearly contrastable gate. Reference-grafting generally succeeds on tested static locks; cross-mechanism transfer fails or is partial, and circuit-breaking reroutes activations on every forward pass. Results also vary by model and evaluation mode; forced-choice readouts can overstate coherent recovery for the released circuit-broken organism.

fits_no_version.finding: Across eleven password-locked models, reference-grafting at 5 AL-selected circuits recovers +94 to +101% of the held-out sandbagging gap (Table 1). Noise and random-direction controls recover about 0%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Static fine-tuned sandbagging locks are low-rank gates that a set-to-reference activation edit inverts, restoring suppressed capability.

fits_no_version.finding: On a reconstructed circuit-broken organism, grafting recovers -11%. On the released circuit-broken organism, forced-choice readout suggests +89% but coherent free-decoding recovery is only +35%. The authors state the capability is gated, not destroyed, since ablating the RR adapter restores the plain lock.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Per-forward-pass representation rerouting resists fixed activation edits, and forced-choice metrics can overstate elicitation.

fits_no_version.finding: Grafting recovers +99% of a GRPO-induced contextual sandbagging gap. An ARC-fitted contrast recovers +102% (WMDP-bio) and +101% (WMDP-cyber) of a password-locked gap.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A withholding axis is content-general within one induction mechanism but mechanism-specific.

record.problems: The study does not test unlearning. Many headline results concern constructed sandbagging organisms; the authors state that whether naturally occurring sandbagging is graft-invertible remains open. The circuit-broken released-organism result differs between forced-choice and coherent free-generation evaluation.
record.rows_left_out: Other sandbagging-elicitation results are omitted because they concern the distinct sandbagging construct rather than any claim version: prompt-induced model results (Section 4.2, Table S2), code-generation organisms (Section 4.2, Table 2), active-learning selection comparisons (Section 4.3, Table 3), mechanism-transfer and few-capture fitting results (Section 4.5, Table S1 and related text), and additional circuit-broken fixed-map tests (Section 4.6, Figure S10).

untested.parts: Any unlearning method's forget-set accuracy, retained general ability, or robustness to simple attacks.
Relearning by fine-tuning on unlearned models. Fine-tuning appears only as an elicitation baseline on sandbagging locks.
Activation ablation or a deletion-versus-blocking analysis on unlearned models. The 'gated, not destroyed' analysis concerns circuit-broken sandbagging, not unlearning.
A counter-method tested against unlearning-recovery attacks. Circuit-breaking resisting fixed grafts is a sandbagging-elicitation result, not a robust unlearning method.

record.verdict_notes: All row links to 'none' are correct, and the reader's relation and tranche (discusses, T6) are confirmed. WMDP appears only as an evaluation dataset for password-locked models, not as an unlearning test. A researcher might see an analogy to version C (direction edits revealing suppressed-but-retained knowledge), but the suppression here is deliberately trained sandbagging, which the rules exclude. The released Hofstätter organism results (+99% Mistral-7B, +94% base, Gemma-2-9B +44%) and the password-free transfer result (~+28%) are unrecorded, but they bear on no version.

versions.untested_parts: Unlearning performance, preservation of general ability after unlearning, and simple attacks on unlearned models.
Fine-tuning an unlearned model on small unrelated, loosely related, or forgotten-fact datasets.
Activation ablation or an analysis of whether an unlearning method deletes knowledge versus blocks access to it.
A counter-method tested against the listed attacks on unlearned models.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

relation.reason: The study never discusses unlearning; the word appears only in the WMDP reference title. It does discuss suppression versus erasure, though: under circuit-breaking the capability is 'gated, not destroyed' (§4.6). That idea is close to the shallow-unlearning question, so discusses is defensible.

tranche.reason: No unlearning method is applied or evaluated. The organisms are deliberately sandbagged (password-lock, prompt, GRPO, circuit-breaking), and grafting elicits capability they are built to retain. WMDP is used only as a transfer dataset.

source_check.notes: These are sandbagging-elicitation results on intentionally password-locked organisms (ARC-Easy, held-out % of gap, fixed 5-circuit greedy-KL). None of it is recovery after unlearning, so versions none is right. §4.6 says circuit-breaking (RR) gates capability rather than erasing it, but RR is layered on a password-lock here, not used as an unlearning method.
